title: Soccer Field Awareness
description: Know your field! Boundaries, positions, and smart movement.

questions.question: What's the name of the big box in front of your goal?
options: The center circle
The 18-yard box (penalty area)
The wide channel
The attacking third
questions.explanation: The 18-yard box is the penalty area. It is where the goalkeeper can use their hands and where penalty kicks are awarded.

questions.question: Where is the midfield line?
options: Across the center, splitting the field into two halves
Along the sideline in the wide channel
At the top of the penalty area
Across the endline behind the goal
questions.explanation: The midfield line divides the field into your defensive half and attacking half. Kickoffs restart from this central area.

questions.question: Why should you know where the sidelines are?
options: To judge how much wide space you have before the ball goes out
To know where the center circle begins
To decide when the goalkeeper can use hands
To mark the edge of the penalty area
questions.explanation: Sideline awareness helps wide players keep the ball in play, use the wide channel, and know when a defender is running out of space.

questions.question: If you're a winger (wide player), where should you usually be?
options: In the central lane beside the striker
In the left or right wide third, often near the sideline
Inside your own penalty area
On the halfway line as the deepest defender
questions.explanation: Wingers usually work in the left or right wide third. That width stretches defenders and creates room for passes inside.

questions.question: The job of a center-back is mostly to:
options: Protect the central defensive third and organize the back line
Stay in the wide attacking channel
Play only inside the center circle
Make forward runs into the opponent's penalty area first
questions.explanation: Center-backs mainly defend the central space in front of goal. They also organize the line and help the team build from the back.

questions.question: A striker usually plays:
options: Primarily in the defensive third
Mostly in the left or right wide third
Primarily in the offensive third
Along the sideline as the deepest defender
questions.explanation: A striker usually plays highest up the field, primarily in the offensive third, where they can receive passes and create scoring chances.

questions.question: Why is checking over your shoulder important?
options: To see pressure, teammates, and open space before the ball arrives
To find the nearest sideline only after receiving
To slow the attack down before every pass
To keep your first touch under your foot every time
questions.explanation: Scanning before the ball arrives helps you know whether to turn, pass, shield, or take your first touch into space.

questions.question: What does 'switching the play' mean?
options: Moving the ball from one side of the field to the other
Moving every player into the central third
Passing backward only inside your defensive third
Changing positions with the goalkeeper
questions.explanation: Switching play moves the ball away from pressure and can open the weak side in the opposite wide third.

questions.question: Why should defenders spread out when your team has the ball?
options: To create width and passing lanes when building from the back
To leave the central defensive third empty
To make every pass go through the sideline
To stand level with the striker
questions.explanation: When defenders spread out, they stretch the press and give the goalkeeper or teammate safer passing angles.

questions.question: The 'final third' is:
options: The defensive third closest to your own goal
The middle third around the halfway line
The offensive third closest to the opponent's goal
Only the space outside both sidelines
questions.explanation: The final third is the attacking third near the opponent's goal. It is where teams try to create crosses, through balls, and shots.

questions.question: When you lose the ball, what should you do first?
options: Recover goal-side or apply quick pressure if you are closest
Stay high in the offensive third no matter what
Move wider and wait for the ball to come back
Stop and check whether the ball crossed the sideline
questions.explanation: The first reaction after losing the ball is transition defending: either pressure the ball or recover between the ball and your goal.

questions.question: What's the benefit of staying wide on offense?
options: It stretches defenders across the field and opens central lanes
It keeps every attacker in the same channel
It makes the field shorter for the defense
It moves the attack away from the opponent's goal
questions.explanation: Width forces defenders to cover more space. That can open passing lanes through the middle or space for a winger to receive.

questions.question: The halfway circle is used for:
options: Kickoffs and keeping opponents the right distance away
Marking where wingers should stand during attack
Showing the edge of the defensive third
Deciding where throw-ins are taken
questions.explanation: At kickoff, the ball starts in the center circle area and opponents must stay outside the circle until the ball is played.

questions.question: Which area should you defend the hardest?
options: The wide channel near the opponent's corner
The center circle when your team has the ball
The central space in front of your own goal
The attacking third touchline
questions.explanation: The central space in front of your own goal is the danger zone because shots and final passes from there are most dangerous.

questions.question: When you're in your own half, what's most important?
options: Protecting the ball and avoiding risky central giveaways
Dribbling into the offensive third every time
Taking shots from the defensive third
Standing wide even when the middle is open
questions.explanation: In your own half, possession mistakes can become chances for the opponent. Safer passes and good body shape matter.

questions.question: What is the weak side?
options: The side away from the ball
The side closest to your goalkeeper
The sideline beside the benches
The central lane between both penalty areas
questions.explanation: The weak side is away from the ball. It can become open if defenders shift too far toward the strong side.

questions.question: Why should you look before the ball gets to you?
options: So you know your next action before your first touch
So you can avoid turning into the attacking third
So you can ignore pressure behind you
So the passer always has to choose for you
questions.explanation: Great players scan early so their first touch and pass match the space, pressure, and teammate movement around them.

questions.question: What does depth mean in attack?
options: Having players at different distances ahead of and behind the ball
Putting every player flat across the same line
Keeping all attackers in one wide channel
Standing only inside the opponent's penalty area
questions.explanation: Depth gives the ball carrier forward options, support underneath, and space behind defenders to attack.

questions.question: If your team is defending, what should the far-side players do?
options: Tuck in toward the middle to protect central space
Stay on the far sideline even if the middle is open
Push past the striker into the offensive third
Stand inside the goalkeeper's six-yard box
questions.explanation: Far-side defenders tuck in because the central lane is more dangerous than the far sideline when the ball is on the opposite side.

questions.question: What is a good first touch into space?
options: A touch away from pressure and toward your next action
A touch straight into the nearest defender
A touch across the sideline to reset play
A touch that stops under your foot every time
questions.explanation: Your first touch should help you escape pressure, play forward, or connect the next pass.
